He asked me to send it before Friday.
I have four minutes before my next call. What happened?
Three things. They said they could accept twelve months on the cap. They were adamant that fraud stays outside it. And they asked whether we had already spoken to the board.
Did they say twelve, or did they say they could live with twelve?
Her words were that twelve was something she could take to her client. So it is not agreed. I am relaying that as she said it, because the difference matters on Friday.
Good. And what do you think is actually going on?
That part is my reading, not theirs. She was guarded about the timetable and open about everything else, and she downplayed the delay twice. My reading is that their board meets before ours does.
Did she actually say that, or is that you?
That is me. She never mentioned a board meeting. She hinted at a date twice and walked it back both times, and the note I send you tonight will say exactly that, in two separate paragraphs.
They said that they could accept twelve months on the cap.
She asked whether we had spoken to the board.
She was adamant that fraud stays outside the cap.
They told me that, and my reading of it is this.
That is my reading. She did not say it.

What I want from an external lawyer after a meeting is three sentences, and I want them in a particular order. What was agreed, what was not agreed, and what you think they will do next. That third one is the one people leave out, because it is the only part that is a judgement rather than a record, and nobody wants to be wrong in writing. I would rather have you wrong in writing than silent. The other thing I ask for, and I have to ask every time, is that you separate what they said from what you concluded. If your note tells me they were unwilling to move on the cap, I need to know whether they said that in those words or whether you watched somebody hesitate for two seconds and drew a conclusion. Both are useful to me. They are not the same thing, and by Thursday nobody remembers which one it was.

There is a sentence I have started using and it has saved me more than once. When I report a meeting now I say, they told me X, and my reading of it is Y. Two clauses, and a visible seam between them. For years I did not do that, and what happened is what happens to everybody. You compress. You take the four things somebody said, plus their tone, plus the fact that they arrived late and looked tired, and you produce one confident sentence: they are not going to sign. And you are usually right, which is the dangerous part, because the one time in eight when you are wrong, nobody can reconstruct how the conclusion was reached, including you. Now I write the two halves separately, and if the second half turns out to be nonsense, at least the first half is still true and the client can work from it.
